The '''dabus''' (pronounciation: DAH-buss, [[File:PronounceDabus.ogg|200px]]<ref name="audiodabus">[https://web.archive.org/web/20000818060140/http://www.wizards.com/dnd/DnDDownloads_prev.asp WotC Downloads page, retrieved Aug 12 2000]</ref>) are the mysterious servants of the [[Lady of Pain]] and the caretakers of [[Sigil]]. Tall gaunt figures with grayish skin, a shock of white hair, and goat horns, they float several inches above the ground.
They communicate exclusively via rebus, a visual puzzle that hovers in the air. The rebuses themselves appear to be crafted in [[Planar Common]].
Dabus may be related to the [[phirblas]] of the [[Ethereal plane]], who have a similar appearance, but their words appear plainly written in the air rather than being encoded into a rebus.
Some dabus found their way to [[Logicus]] where they were adapted into [[programmer]]s, whose speech takes the form of hovering mathematical formulae.<ref name="dttu52">{{b|Planescape|Doors to the Unknown|pdf=17290|page=52}}</ref>

[[File:DarkSunLogo2e.png|500px|center|Dark Sun]]
'''Dark Sun''' is a [[Dungeons & Dragons]] Campaign Setting.
''Dark Sun'' takes place in the world of [[Athas]], in the [[Prime Material plane]]. The world is predominantly a desert, water and metal is scarce, and life is harsh. Long ago a great magical ritual drained power from the blue sun, aging it rapidly and warming the planet's surface. Now it sits, swollen and red, overlooking the desert.
While many worlds have a great conflict between the gods and the titans, Athas is one of the cases in which the titans won. The titans then sealed Athas' crystal sphere such that the gods could not return. As a result, Athas' "clerics" instead worship elemental entities from the Inner Planes. Their sorcerous magic is not drawn from an external source, such a god of magic, but is instead converted from local life energy. As a result, two kinds of wizard have arisen: defilers, who will drain everything dry in order to power their spells, and preservers, who seek to draw smaller amounts from a wider area, in order that the life might continue to live.
Life is focused on a few major city-states, ruled over by the dangerous dragon-kings.
== Dark Sun and the Planes == As noted, Athas' crystal sphere was reinforced by the world's titans long ago. The effects are many: Athas' crystal sphere cannot be physically entered, passage to and from the Astral or Outer planes is rare (albeit not impossible), and the Border Ethereal has been replaced entirely by a feature called "The Gray." If one enters the Gray, they become lost, although if they are lucky, might leave at the same point they entered. This means travelers from the Deep Ethereal cannot pass into Athas, nor can travelers from Athas enter the Deep Ethereal.
Although oddly, due to the prevalence of elemental priests, summonings and other contact with the Inner Planes works as normal, despite the Gray.
Most of the multiverse recognizes the four para-elemental planes as [[Frostfell (plane)|Ice]] (between Air and Water), [[Fountains of Creation|Magma]] (between Fire and Earth), [[Swamp of Oblivion|Ooze]] (between Earth and Water), and [[Great Conflagration|Smoke]] (between Air and Fire). Curiously, however, Athasians instead recognize Magma, Rain (Air and Water), Silt (Earth and Water), and Sun (Air and Fire). It's not known if they're accessing specific parts of the known para-elemental planes, if they're mis-labeling known quasi-elemental planes ([[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Radiance|Radiance]] as Sun, for example), or if they've discovered a new set of planes entirely.

[[File:DayofGrace.jpg|300px|right|thumb|A dramatic depiction of the first Grace]] The '''Day of Grace''' (or often just '''Grace''') is a holiday that marks the beginning of a new year on [[Sigil]]'s [[timeline|calendar]]. Everyone shows grace, mercy, and forgiveness. There are no floggings or other punishments, no public executions. Cagers are expected to forgive innocent mistakes. Rumor has it that those who refuse to observe Grace risk the Lady's attention.
== History == According to the tales, long ago in Sigil's history, the [[Lady of Pain]] was floating through the city, as she sometimes does. The streets often empty out when the Lady passes by: no one wants to risk earning her ire and be caught in her gaze or her shadow.
But on this day, a young girl with a big smile on her face ran up to the Lady. She spoke something to the Lady. Some claim that the child's words softened Her Serenity's heart, others claim that the Lady didn't even notice the girl. But the Lady showed the young girl grace, and she survived the encounter.
What the girl spoke, or what came of her afterwards, no one knows.
The people of Sigil were moved, and set up a celebration in remembrance. If the Lady showed grace on that day, then Cagers all across the city should too. It marks the beginning of the year, as [[Fraternity of Order|Guvner]] calendars reckon it.
== Observance ==
At first light on the Day of Grace, the Harmonium marches through [[The Lady's Ward]]. It began as a celebration but (of course) has evolved into more of a military exercise.
Later in the day, the [[Palace of the Jester]] hosts a grand masquerade ball, attended by over a thousand of the city's social elite. Each year's ball is hosted by a different family, and the competition between families plays out as each one tries to outdo the previous year's celebration.
Many merchants offer sales or discounts, so Cagers take the opportunity to purchase gifts for their friends.
=== Factions ===
* [[Athar]] claim that the day shows that grace comes not from powers, but from mortals. * Similarly, the [[Bleak Cabal]] say that the only true meaning comes from individual action. * [[Believers of the Source]] view the day as a test. * The [[Fated]] see the day as a challenge, as the attitude -- particularly the expectation of debt forgiveness -- does not come easily to them. * [[Doomguard]] and [[Mercykillers]] understandably have a tough time showing mercy. * The [[Harmonium]] and [[Fraternity of Order]], of course, follow all the rules and regs on proper celebration. * The [[Revolutionary League]] generally tries to make sure that their plots don't come to fruition on this day. * The [[Society of Sensation]] tries to think of new ways to show grace every year. * [[Heralds of Dust]], [[Free League]], [[Sign of One]], and [[Transcendent Order]] are typically too occupied with other concerns to pay much attention. * No one's been able to figure out the [[Xaositects]].

==Description== Decatons were shaped like spheres atop stubby legs, with ten tentacles and four eyes evenly spaced around the sphere. At the top of the sphere was a mouth.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /><ref name="MM21e-p89" />
==Abilities== Like all hierarch modrons, decatons had the innate ability to duplicate the effects of ''[[clairaudience]]'', ''[[clairvoyance]]'', ''[[command]]'', ''[[dimension door]]'', ''[[teleport without error]]'', and ''[[wall of force]]'' spells at will.<ref name="TGMM-p126" /> Additionally, they were able to [[cure wounds|cure injuries]] and [[cure disease]]s from all modrons within {{SI|144|ft}} and {{SI|12|ft}}, respectively. They could also [[heal]] and [[remove paralysis]] by physically touching another modron.<ref name="TGMM-p126">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref><ref name="MM21e-p86" />
They could communicate [[telepathy|telepathically]] with anyone in a {{SI|44|mile|long=yes}} radius.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p2" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /> and could see in [[darkvision|complete darkness]] from up to {{SI|44|ft|long=yes}} away.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" />
Decatons were able to fly by generating a lifting gas that allowed it to be lighter than the surrounding air.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /><ref name="MM21e-p86" /> They typically only did so whenever they were commanding large numbers of base modrons and needed to get an overview of their situation.<ref name="MM21e-p86" />
==Combat== If forced into combat, a decaton used its tentacles in melee combat. They also heavily relied on their spellcasting abilities.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" />
==Society== There were only 100 decatons in modron society.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p2" /><ref name="MM21e-p89" /><ref name="MM21e-p86">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|86}}</ref> They could communicate with other decatons and with [[nonaton]]s, and relayed their orders to [[pentadrone]]s.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p2" /> One decaton was in charge of each of the 64 sectors of their realm in [[Mechanus]], and the remaining 36 decatons served in the modron armies. They functioned as caretakers of the modrons under their command,<ref name="MotPWE3e-p10-11" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p2" /><ref name="MM21e-p89" /> looking after their physical welfare.<ref name="MM21e-p89" /><ref name="MM21e-p86" />
Decatons were always created as the result of pentadrones being upgraded to take the place of destroyed or further promoted decatons.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p2-3">{{Cite web enhancement/The Modrons|2-3}}</ref>
==History== Around {{Yearlink|-346}} [[Netheril|Netherese]] [[archmage]] and explorer Lady [[Polaris]] came upon Mechanus and the modrons. She [[Gate|summoned]] several decatons to her home to guard her treasures, but was stymied as they kept disappearing after several days. She had more success with the pentadrones she focused on next.<ref>{{Cite book/How the Mighty Are Fallen|3, 31}}</ref>

==Cosmology== In the [[Great Wheel cosmology]], this realm was located within the larger realm of [[Tir na Og]] in the [[Outlands]].<ref name="OHG2e-p75,181" /><ref name="FA2e-p145" /> According to the [[World Tree cosmology]], the realm was located in the [[House of Nature]].<ref name="PGF3e-p158-159" /> And the [[World Axis cosmology]] placed this realm in the [[Deep Wilds]].<ref name="FRCG4e-p63" /><ref name="Dr367-p59" />
==Geography== The Deep Forest was home to the greatest of all trees. It was a realm of thick and feral vegetation, as well as a rich and diverse wildlife. Dense and majestic canopies almost entirely blocked sunlight from reaching the ground below.<ref name="OHG2e-p75,181" /><ref name="PGF3e-p158-159" />
The entire place was claimed by nature. There were no artificial buildings anywhere in the Deep Forest.<ref name="FRCG4e-p63" />
==Notable Locations== Silvanus was said to make his home at the heart of the Deep Forest, in a glen that was also referred to as Summeroak.<ref name="Dr367-p59" />

{{Plane | image = | caption = | name = The Demiplane of Imprisonment | othernames = | symbol = | demonym = | natives = | languages = | basicrefs = | type-GW = [[Demiplane]]<ref name="D353-MD" /> | shape-size-GW = Finite<ref name="D353-MD" /> | gravity-GW = None<ref name="D353-MD" /> | time-GW = No Time<ref name="D353-MD" /> | morphic-GW = Divinely Morphic<ref name="D353-MD" /> | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = Mildly Evil Aligned<ref name="D353-MD" /> | magical-GW = No Magic<ref name="D353-MD" /> | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = | refs-GW = | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = | magical-WT = | faith-WT = | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = | inhabitants = | deities = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = | useon = }} The '''Demiplane of Imprisonment''' was an extremely obscure [[demiplane]]. Very little was known about it.<ref name="D353-MD">{{Cite dragon/353/Multiple Dementia: A Guide to the Demiplanes}}</ref>
==Geography== The demiplane resembled a crystalline cyst floating through the Ethereal Plane. The ether for {{SI|500|feet|long=yes}} around the demiplane continuously manifested dreamscapes for the nightmares that an intelligence within sent around the multiverse to its would-be worshipers; these were dominated by purple eyes, mouths, veined whirlpools, and dark humanoid figures. The visions continuously attempted to goad, tempt, and seduce travelers into touching the crystal, which would trap them in the demiplane.<ref name="D353-MD" />
==History== Sometime after {{yearlink|-3234}}, the archwizard [[Madryoch]] was banished to this demiplane.<ref name="TGHotR-18" /> The plane was rediscovered later by Netherese arcanists following up on the work of the archmage [[Lord Shadow|Shadow]]; a handful of them became imprisoned in it.<ref name="NEoM-10">{{Cite book/Netheril: Empire of Magic/Encyclopedia Arcana|10}}</ref> Shadow himself used assassins he caught alive as exploration guinea pigs, making them touch its surface; he never managed to retrieve them afterwards.<ref name="RotA">{{cite book/Realms of the Arcane|194}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== People who touched the crystal were absorbed into the demiplane. No one could leave on their own power; it took a spell like ''[[wish]]'' or ''[[miracle]]'' from someone outside the demiplane to escape. Those removed would be under the effects of an ''[[insanity]]'', that could be healed in the same ways as the effects of the spell of the same name.<ref name="D353-MD" />
The archwizard Madryoch had been banished to this demiplane.<ref name="TGHotR-18">{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|18}}</ref> Madryoch's essence later escaped the imprisonment, instead being trapped in the [[Plane of Shadow]].<ref name="TSS-C18">{{Cite book/The Shadow Stone||18}}</ref>
==Legends== The Demiplane of Imprisonment was a legend even to the gods. According to its legend, an irredeemably evil creature and its servants had been banished from all of reality to the [[Negative Material Plane]] by the gods that came before the gods, with this demiplane housing remnants of their forces.<ref name="MotP1-21">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|21}}</ref>
The color of this demiplane's ethereal curtain was unrecorded. Travelers were recommended not to cross color pools of unrecognized color, lest they accidentally find themselves here.<ref name="GttEP">{{Cite book/A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|20, 46}}</ref> Most realms had similar legends about a demiplane of this nature, with the local theology substituted, having all come together to imprison there what remnants of the evil force they could not or would not completely annihilate.<ref name="D353-MD" />

{{Plane | image = | caption = | name = Demiplane of Nightmares | othernames = | natives = [[Diabolus|Diaboli]], the [[Night Parade]] | languages = | basicrefs = | type-GW = [[Demiplane]] | shape-size-GW = | gravity-GW = | time-GW = | morphic-GW = | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = | magical-GW = | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = | refs-GW = <ref name="AGttEP"/> | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = | magical-WT = | faith-WT = | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = | inhabitants = | deities = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = | useon = }} The '''Demiplane of Nightmares''' was a horrific [[demiplane]] inhabited by creatures that looked like monsters out of nightmares.<ref name="AGttEP">{{Cite book/A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|47}}</ref>
==Description== The Demiplane of Nightmares was a strange place of strange angles and stranger geometry that seemed unsettling, even repulsive, to people from the Material plane.<ref name="AGttEP"/>
The Demiplane of Nightmares was variously described to be either an independent demiplane in the [[Ethereal plane]],<ref name="AGttEP"/> or a demiplane located coterminously with both the [[Region of Dreams]] and the Ethereal Plane. Either way, the boundary between the Demiplane and the [[Far Realm]] was extremely thin and the taint of the latter constantly seeped into the Demiplane, corrupting it.<ref name="D327">{{Cite dragon/327/Winning Races: Diaboli|62-63}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== Creatures known to inhabit the Demiplane of Nightmares included [[neh-thalggu]], [[diabolus|diaboli]], [[feyr]]s, [[nagpa]]s, and [[maelephant]]s. Of these, only the diaboli were actually native to the demiplane.<ref name="MMC-26">{{Cite book/Monstrous Compendium Mystara Appendix|26}}</ref> The diaboli occupied the same niche on the Demiplane of Nightmares that humans did on the Material Plane.<ref name="D327"/><ref name="MMC-26"/> [[Malfera]]s were a native predator of the demiplane.<ref>{{Cite dragon/343/Creature Collection V|51-52}}</ref>
The creatures that lived in the Demiplane of Nightmares were horrific beings to the eyes of most people. It was said that they saw creatures from the Material plane in much the same way, and certainly the diaboli instinctively feared humans and other humanoids.<ref name="MMC-26"/><ref name="AGttEP"/>
==History== In {{Yearlink|-681}}, [[Netherese]] [[arcanist]]s emigrated to the Demiplane of Nightmares, where the energies infusing the plane twisted their descendants until they evolved into the [[Night Parade]].<ref name="LEoF-98">{{Cite book/Lost Empires of Faerûn|98}}</ref>
Around and prior to the year {{Yearlink|1359}}, members of the Night Parade opened ''[[portal]]s'' back to the Realms, where they began infiltrating cities such as [[Calimport]].<ref>{{Cite book/The Night Parade}}</ref>
==Rumors & Legends== Some claimed that the dark powers must have pulled part of the Demiplane of Nightmare into the [[Demiplane of Dread]] to create an even more terrifying expanse in that place.<ref name="AGttEP"/>

Pearl and silver{{Cite book/A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|20}} | basicrefs = | type-GW = [[Demiplane]] | shape-size-GW = Finite | gravity-GW = | time-GW = Flowing, erratic | morphic-GW = | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = | magical-GW = Impeded | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = the [[Ethereal Plane]] | refs-GW = | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = | magical-WT = | faith-WT = | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = | inhabitants = | deities = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = | useon = }} The '''Demiplane of Time''',{{Cite book/Chronomancer|88}}{{Cite dragon/353/Multiple Dementia: A Guide to the Demiplanes|39}} or '''Demi-Plane of Time''', also called the '''Plane of Time''', '''Temporal Energy Plane''', '''Time Plane'''{{Cite book/Monster Manual II 1st edition|120-121}} or the '''Temporal Prime''', was a [[demiplane]]Although those aware of its presence in [[Toril]], and even [[chronomancer]]s beyond, referred to the Temporal Prime as a demiplane, many chronomancers swore that it was in fact more technically similar to a "dimensional plane" or "dimension". Such a difference was very difficult for most to understand, as scholars would try to fit the "plane" into their cosmological theories. Most cosmologists still referred to the Demiplane of Time as a demiplane{{Cite book/Chronomancer|4}} of the [[Ethereal Plane]]. ==Description== The Demiplane of Time was an extradimensional space that could allow travelers to move through time, i.e., [[time travel]]. Very little was truly known about this ethereal demiplane, and despite diligent research, there were still too many inaccuracies and contradictions from "first-hand" accounts to conclude what was true, and what was not.{{Cite book/A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|50}} There were several different ways to describe the Demiplane of Time. Some believed it was a pocket dimension set aside from the rest of the multiverse, whilst others believed it was a plane that overlayed the [[Prime Material plane]]. [[File:Chrono29.png|thumb|right|''Adventurers escape a [[vortex spider]], as they move towards a temporal vortex.'']] Although not much was known for certain, and many had differing views, it was generally agreed that the place was dark, and permeated with a blue-gray mist. Threads and lines flowed through the vast darkness, which some believed to be timelines of living beings. It was also generally considered to be very dangerous, and could age those who passed through it considerably.{{Cite book/Tales of the Outer Planes|12-15}}{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|208-210}} ===Place in Traditional Cosmology=== In traditional cosmology, the Demi-Plane of Time was a large dimensional demiplane that operated by its own rules. It appeared to be almost as large as the [[Demiplane of Shadow]], and its temporal manifestations extended into its Border Ethereal. It was hostile to life, but housed a few native species, such as [[vortex spider]]s. The curtain that surrounded the dimensional plane was semi-transparent, but had shadowy shapes that appeared beyond it. It did not show up on [[Great Wheel cosmology]] diagrams, the same with other demiplanes, as the properties of the extradimensional space were constantly changing with time.{{Cite book/Planar Handbook|135-138}} ===Chronomancers' Viewpoint=== Many [[chronomancer]]s believed that the Demiplane of Time, which they called the Temporal Prime, was a dimension in which ''timestreams'' could be observed and used to move through time. Timestreams were formed by currents in time-space, which themselves were formed by the lifelines of living beings. However, these were not always stable, and thus could be turbulent, forming temporal vortices, allowing travel from one reality to another. The plane looked like an infinitely large dark space, with only timestreams illuminating its vast darkness.{{Cite book/Chronomancer|19}} ==Laws== {{fq |text=What exists may be exploited. If power can be drawn from the elements, what kind of [[magic]] could be made possible by tapping a dimension? |source=Excerpt from ''Theories of Time'' }} The Temporal Prime, naturally, temporally affected those who went to or from it. After coming back from the plane, many found themselves either younger or older. Substances that were created could not permanently exist on the demiplane, as the [[magic]]al laws that created matter were very weak there. As such, both [[arcane]] and [[divine]] [[spell]]s involving some form of matter (such as ''[[fog cloud]]'' and ''[[create water]]''), would be impeded.{{Cite book/Chronomancer|67-70}} ==Importance in the Realms== The Temporal Prime was known to many [[deities]], [[sage]]s, and [[wizard]]s of the [[Realms]], who generally knew it as the Plane, or Demiplane, of Time. The demiplane was highly important to those such as [[Elminster Aumar]], the [[Seven Sisters]], and [[Khelben Arunsun]]. [[Mystra]] had granted them powers to prevent [[chronomancer]]s from meddling with the temporal demiplane, which could potentially destroy history. If a chronomancer severely interrupted the timeline of events in [[Toril]], they would be quickly and efficiently destroyed by an avatar of a deity. As it was in the deities' interests to keep history complete and unbroken, [[Oghma]] and [[Deneir]] bestowed similar supernatural powers unto their followers. The Oghmanyte and Deneirrath priests were said to be able to follow the path of chronomancers through the Plane of Time and reverse the potential damage. As such, chronomancers made very limited voyages through time in [[Faerûn]], [[Kara-Tur]], [[Zakhara]], and [[Maztica]]. Vortex spiders, denizens of the Time Plane, were known to have rarely appeared in [[Faerûn]].{{Cite game/Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal}} ==Rumors & Legends== * No one that had entered the plane was known to return. However, there were rumors that time-[[mage]]s, known as chronomancers had mastered the art of traveling up and down the cords of time. * In the [[Gates of the Moon]], the [[divine realm]] of [[Selûne]], one could find sand allegedly from "the shores" of this plane, though merchants would never reveal how they managed to reach the Demiplane of Time.{{Cite book/Planes of Chaos/The Book of Chaos|117}} ==Appendix== ===Notes=== {{Notes}} ===References=== {{Refs}} [[Category:Demiplanes]]

[[Sigil]] has no cardinal directions as most primes are familiar with them. Directions are instead given in terms of wards and directions related to the [[Spire]].
While a "up" on a prime map may represent North, most who read it understand that North is not literally up, away from their world's center of gravity. But recalling that Sigil is floating on its side in relation to the [[Outlands]], one side of the map would quite literally be up.
'''Spikeward''' represents this upward direction, the edge of Sigil furthest away from the [[Spire]] and the [[Outlands]]. The opposite edge is '''Downward''' (although '''Spireward''' is sometimes used<ref name="poly155-14">{{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 155|page=144}}</ref>).
[[Fraternity of Order]] surveyors also sometimes use additional terms: '''Radial''' indicates locations on the opposite side of Sigil, if you were to draw a straight line through the middle to the part of the city hanging directly over your head. [[The Lady's Ward]] is Radial to the [[Clerk's Ward]], for example. '''Chordwise''' is close-to-Radial -- the Lady's Ward is Chordwise to the [[Guildhall Ward]] and the [[Hive Ward]]. Both of those terms are, however, more typically applied to individual locations and not entire Wards, so Chordwise in practice is usually a narrower cone than the examples given.
== Background Information ==
* Although never defined, it's likely that there would be some need for an East/West equivalent as well. One option is to assume that Sigil slowly spins -- perhaps one full spin per month, or one per year. Walking Sigil in the direction of the spin would be '''Spinwise''' while the opposite direction would be '''Dragward''', implying you're trying to slow down time by walking the "wrong" way. * Many NPCs in ''[[Planescape: Torment]]'' use traditional cardinal directions -- northwest exit, building to the south, etc -- relying on most gamers' typical assumptions of "north" being towards the top of the screen, and other directions following suit.

Prior to the [[Spellplague]] it was known as '''Deep Caverns''' in the [[World Tree cosmology]] model.<ref name="PGtF-140" /> It was the home plane of the [[Great Mother]], [[Ilsensine]], [[Laogzed]],<ref name="PGtF-149">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|149}}</ref> and [[Ghaunadaur]].<ref name="FRCG4e-63" />
==Description== This plane was a great solid mass of rock perforated by caverns, chasms, and tunnels of all sizes. There was no sky and no light<ref name="PGtF-148" /> except for that given off by luminous fungi and molten lava flows.<ref name="FRCG4e-63" /> Portions of the Caverns were subject to swift winds that howled through the maze of tunnels.<ref name="PGtF-148" /> Mapping the labyrinth of tunnels was completely impossible because within the demesnes of the deities the passageways and walls obeyed their will and could open, close, change direction, or collapse on an infernal whim.<ref name="PGtF-148-149">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|148-149}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== Dismal Caverns was the [[afterlife]] destination of most [[beholder]], [[illithid]], and [[troglodyte]] petitioners, and they appeared here much the same as they had in life. Their behavior was also similar as in their former lives and the disparate groups viewed each other with disdain, hatred, or animosity.<ref name="PGtF-148" /> [[Ooze]]s, [[slime]]s, and [[abomination]]s of all kinds also gathered here under the lurking eye of Ghaunadaur.<ref name="FRCG4e-74">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|74}}</ref> The constant howling and particularly desolate and mournful tone of the winds that blew through regions of the Dismal Caverns attracted many [[howler]]s from their native [[Supreme Throne]].<ref name="PGtF-148" />
==Realms== The realms of the most powerful inhabitants were widely separated because of the dislike and distrust between their rulers and it was difficult to determine where one domain ended and another began.<ref name="PGtF-148" /> *'''[[Ghaunadaur]]''', the Elder Eye, once a member of the [[Dark Seldarine|Drow Pantheon]], retreated to this plane from the [[Demonweb Pits]] in the [[1379 DR|Year of the Lost Keep, 1379 DR]].<ref name="GHotR-159">{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|159}}</ref> He was fed up with the machinations of the [[drow]] goddess [[Lolth]] and slunk away in order to rebuild his worshiper base.<ref name="FRCG4e-74" /> * The '''[[Great Mother]]''' of the [[beholder]]s had a large demesne known as the [[Realm of a Million Eyes]] on this plane. She lived in a vast cave at the bottom of a region permeated by vertical shafts, which suited her floating petitioners and offspring. Her spawning ground was inviolable because she ate anyone who approached too closely, including her own children.<ref name="PGtF-149" /> * '''[[Ilsensine]]''', the god of the [[mind flayer]]s, ruled over the [[Caverns of Thought]] somewhere on this plane. This area echoed with its thoughts, so evil that every thinking creature eventually went mad.<ref name="PGtF-149" /> * '''[[Laogzed]]''', the nearly mindless god of the [[troglodyte]]s, scavenged the [[Rotting Plain]]—a huge cavern scattered with noisome lakes and ponds fed through myriad tunnels by the [[River of Blood]] which washed all the effluvium of the [[Fiendish planes]] through here,<ref name="PGtF-149" /> on its way to the [[Fated Depths]].<ref name="PGtF-141">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|141}}</ref> Laogzed's insatiable hunger caused him to eat everything he found, be it animal, vegetable, or mineral.<ref name="PGtF-149" />

[[File:DitchMap.png|right|300px|Ditch map]] The '''Ditch''' is [[Sigil]]'s largest body of "water", and crosses the city nearly directly spikeward/downward. It's widely considered the boundary between the [[Lower Ward]] and the [[Hive Ward]], although most place the Ditch itself within the Lower Ward.
The Ditch is 50' wide drainage aqueduct, which some say is a tributary of the [[River Styx]]. It's frequently used as a dumping ground for Cagers looking for an easy way to get rid of refuse, or a body that's been asking too many questions. The waters are heavily polluted and corrosive, partly due to their extra-planar origin, partly because it's also used by the [[Great Foundry]] for their waste runoff. A corpse thrown in the Ditch will be unrecognizable in a matter of hours. Every five-to-eight months, water from the [[River Oceanus]] pours through, clearing out the Ditch and bringing fresh water. This is often a time for celebration, with children playing in the waters for the brief time before the river becomes too corroded once aain.
People can avoid the Ditch between the Lower Ward and Hive by passing spikeward of it, or crossing one of a few bridges. The downward end falls directly off Sigil's edge. Other methods of crossing include the [[Fhurling Bridge]]<ref name="fm124">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=124}}</ref> and the [[Bridge That Spans Worlds]].
Most of Sigil's portals require walking through, but there's still a great need for for various shipping and transport services operating on a larger scale, and that typically requires transport by water. Accordingly, for all its faults, the Ditch is an important part of Sigil's commercial infrastructure.
== Nearby ==
Locations on the banks of the Ditch include:
* The [[Black Sails]] tavern * The [[Styx Oarsman]] saloon * The [[Speckled Rat]] bar * The entrance to the [[Bones of the Night]]<ref name="itc4849">{{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274|page=48-49}}</ref>
== Trade ==
The most important feature of the Ditch is the [[Seafarer's Arch]], a portal formed under the the Bridge That Spans Worlds. It's seemingly unique in Sigil, what [[Lissandra]] the Gate-Seeker has termed a "multiportal." Any number of gate keys can activate the portal, but each gate key goes to a different location. Portals are two-way. Boats travelling the Ditch tend to have the key in a special basket -- a "spritcage" -- attached to the ship's bowsprit. Known destinations (and keys) include:
* A waterfall in Cariele on [[Aebrynis]] * The Silt Sea on [[Athas]] * [[Io's Blood Isles]] * The rapids below a canyon in the Khalkist Mountains on [[Krynn]] * [[Mystara]]'s Savage Coast: a cinnabryl amulet * An oblong shoal of rocks in the Nyv Dyr on [[Oerth]] * [[Ortho]] * The [[Rock of Bral]] * A sewer pipe from [[Toril]]'s Underdeep into the Trackless Sea * [[Amun-Thys]]: a scarab (since the layer is a desert, most ships are marooned and unable to return)
Upstream, ships wishing to trade must pass through the [[Taker's Lock]], a series of watertight doors designed to get ships past a shallow part of the Ditch. Adjacent to the Lock are the [[Industrial Stitches]], a complex series of tracks for transporting raw materials and goods into out out of the Foundry, and a major source of the waste which gets dumped into the Ditch.
== Other Features ==
[[Suicide Falls]] is the downward terminus of the Ditch, where the waters fall outside of Sigil's walls. This is the easiest place to go beyond Sigil's edge. Not a waterfall in the traditional sense, as the water and anything contained in it that pour over the edge just disappears.
The delta near the falls contains a series of small "islands," one of which contains the [[Last Kiss Blossom]], whose petals look like two lips pursed together in a kiss.
[[Arcane Remains]] are the remains of the first ship to enter Sigil via the Seafarer's Arch, a ship full of [[arcane]]. The ship was too wide for the Ditch, and blocked it. Within moments, the [[Lady of Pain]] appeared, her shadow slicing the boat apart to allow for traffic once again. It's now widely known that the arcane are not welcome in Sigil (although not directly barred from entry like powers). Most are afraid to touch the ship's remains, so they continue to sit in the Ditch, rotting and exposed.
The arcane's ship did not go down without a fight, of course. They brought to bear enough power both in magic and in traditional weaponry -- the ship's bombard was considerable -- that the conflagration is said to have been heard out to the gate-towns. The attack, the story goes, did what no one else had managed to do: wound the Lady. One of the blades ringing her head fell off, point-first into the Ditch. What is known, at least, is existence of the [[Knife in the River]], a slowly rusting triangle of still-sharp metal, only a few meters from the Arcane Remains.
At night, near antipeak, when the water's at its murkiest, some Cagers claim to see some sort of '''[[Ditch Beast]]''' in the waters, which they've dubbed "Cassie."
== Background Information == * Most detail on the Ditch comes from the Polyhedron #137 article ''Of Sigil and the Sea.'' The included map had a high-resolution full-color version made and posted to WotC's website as the Map of the Day in 2001. * Lazz highlighted each of the article's sections with a label on the map. Curiously, this includes the "Gate Keys" section, which is about the various gate keys needed to travel through the Seafarer's Arch. Lazz uses this label to point to a sewer outlet. * ''Of Sigil and the Sea'' author [[William James Cuffe]] posted a cut excerpt to his blog, about the [https://livingsigil.wordpress.com/2022/07/17/of-sigil-and-the-sea-forgotten-lore/ Phantom Docks]. Originally intended for the [[Doomguard]]'s [[Ship of Chaos]] project, the docks have lain abandoned for years, although the [[Planar Trade Consortium]] may be repurposing the Ship of Chaos as a terrifying spelljamming ship.

revision.text:
A '''divine realm''' was the personal territory and topographical expression of a [[deity]].<ref name="OHG-54">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|54}}</ref> It served as the deity's work-space, residence, or retreat.<ref name="F&P-9" />
==Description== A divine realm was created by a deity. The material for it was faith. The realm was so completely attuned to the creating god that its state could serve as a mirror for the deity.<ref name="OHG-54" /> For example, when [[Tyr]] had his feud with [[Helm]], the weather in the [[House of the Triad]] became bad.<ref name="TFS-166-182">{{Cite book/The Fractured Sky/Kindle|166-182}}</ref>
However, a divine realm did not necessarily exist in a suitable place for the deity. For example, a god's realm could exist in a place that had nothing to do with the philosophical orientation of the deity. This was because the worshipers' belief, the material out of which the realm was made, and expectations of the god could chain the god and realm to a place that was not necessarily suited for the god.<ref name="OHG-54, 56">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|54, 56}}</ref> However, deities in general preferred to have their realms on the [[Outer Planes]], which were divinely morphic, meaning the deity needed only to exert their will to change the land.<ref name="MotP3e-12">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|12}}</ref>
A number of [[demipower]]s were an exception to these rules: They resided on the [[Prime Material plane]] and nominally considered the whole continent or region of influence of their pantheon their realm, but obviously did not have the kind of control their outer planar counterparts exerted.<ref>{{Cite book/Powers & Pantheons|14, 22, 26, 35-36, 44, 58, 62, 80, 124}}</ref> Some of them had a specific place of power within their claimed area.<ref>{{Cite book/Powers & Pantheons|41, 58, 62, 81-82}}</ref>
==Geography== As mentioned above, deities tended to live on the Outer Planes because they were divinely morphic.<ref name="MotP3e-12" /> Within these realms, deities had absolute control over the physical laws of their realms. In the case of shared realms, this level of absolute control was only enjoyed inside a small part that belonged only to one deity and the borders to other sharing members generally had the physical laws of the [[Material Plane]].<ref name="FRCS3e-256">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|256}}</ref>
===Features=== Divine realms were seemingly infinitely big. This was due to the deities wanting to show grandeur and not because the realms were actually infinitely big.<ref name="OHG-56">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|56}}</ref> A big realm was an indicator of large power, but the reverse was not necessarily true. Deities who preferred not to show-off kept their realms small.<ref name="FRCS3e-256" />
As mentioned above, divinely morphic planes were popular among deities for their mutability in their hands.<ref name="MotP3e-12" /> Even without this trait of a plane, a deity could modify landscape in a drastic manner that depended on the power enjoyed by it.<ref name="F&P-9">{{Cite book/Faiths and Pantheons|9}}</ref>
A [[demigod]] could fill its realm with smells and sounds and also set the temperature as it wished. A [[lesser deity]] could also modify the sound to intelligible speech.<ref name="F&P-9">{{Cite book/Faiths and Pantheons|9}}</ref>
A lesser deity could modify their realm's connection to the [[Astral Plane]] and make particular places inaccessible to teleportation. An [[intermediate deity]] could alter the landscape at will. When it came down to a [[greater deity]], gravity, elemental and energy traits, and even the how flow of time worked were under its control.<ref name="F&P-9" />
An intermediate deity could make their realm strengthen or impede the usage of certain spells while a greater deity could outright ban the use of magic of their choice.<ref name="F&P-9" />
==Government== In general, deities left land and people to their own devices and did little actual ruling, though exceptions existed. The more the deity tended to a ''laissez faire'' attitude, the more traffic was experienced by the realm. Where the god demanded obedience, little traffic took place because of the danger of attracting the deity's ire. The one rule every single realm maintained was to imprison or even kill people who did something that contradicted the dogma of the ruling deity.<ref name="OHG-56" />
==Defenses== Deities could shut out people they did not want coming into their realms, but most relegated the job of keeping out others to [[proxy|proxies]].<ref name="OHG-54" />
==Notable Locations== Divine realms had some places where the ruling god's power was particularly tangible. These holy sites could only be accessed by worshipers of the deity or, in the case of shared realms like [[Tir na Og]], by a worshiper of any of the member gods, as long as it was allowed, something good deities were known to do. These places could give tangible benefits when the faith was real.<ref name="OHG-58">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|58}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== Inhabitants of a divine realm could be split into several categories. ;[[Deity|Deities]] : The deity, or deities in a shared realm, who ruled a divine realm.<ref name="OHG-54" /> ;[[Petitioner]]s : The souls living their afterlifes in their respective deities' realms.<ref name="OHG-56" /> ;Planar beings : People could live in divine realms and did so for generations. A divine realm had less of the problems people had to contend with on the plane outside.<ref name="OHG-57" /> For example, [[Glitterhell]], [[Abbathor]]'s realm, did not have [[Oinos]]'s [[disease]] problem nor the hopelessness due to [[Hades]].<ref name="LM-47, 51">{{Cite book/Planes of Conflict/Liber Malevolentiae|47, 51}}</ref> Another reason people stayed there was faith in the deity, or fear of reprisal from the deity should they leave.<ref name="OHG-57">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|57}}</ref> ;Proxies : Proxies were the representatives of a deity in a divine realm and any visitor was sized up by them on entering a divine realm.<ref name="OHG-57" />

==Description== Some domains were difficult to gain admittance within, often being obscured by an obfuscating barrier or protected by pass phrase, puzzle, or more simply the archfey's discretion.<ref name="DoD-p5" />
==Cosmology== Individual Domains of Delight were accessible from other planes by the same means used to travel to the Feywild, including [[fey crossroad|fey crossings]], and the ''[[plane shift]]'' spell.<ref name="DoD-p17">{{Cite book/Domains of Delight|17}}</ref>
==Geography== The Domains of Delight each varied in size, from the size of a small field to an entire nation,<ref name="DoD-p3" /> depending on the power of the ruling archfey.<ref name="DoD-p5">{{Cite book/Domains of Delight|5}}</ref> The most powerful of the archfey, namely [[Titania]] and the [[Queen of Air and Darkness]], held power that extended well beyond their own Domains of Delight, across nearly the entirety of the Feywild.<ref name="DoD-p12">{{Cite book/Domains of Delight|12}}</ref>
When neighboring domains overlapped with one another, the residents of the contested area were beholden to the authority of each archfey. These instances often led to contention between their respective powers.<ref name="DoD-p5" />
==Inhabitants== Domains of Delight were often home to myriad [[awaken]]ed creatures, [[fey]] creatures, and other rarely-encountered beasts, including: [[boggle]]s, [[brigganock]]s, [[displacer beast]]s, [[harengon]], [[blink dog]]s, [[darkling]]s, [[faerie dragon]]s, various [[hag]]s,<ref name="DoD-p20">{{Cite book/Domains of Delight|20}}</ref> and [[jabberwock]]s.<ref name="DoD-p21">{{Cite book/Domains of Delight|21}}</ref>
==Notable Domains of Delight== * [[Prismeer]], the domain of the archfey [[Zybilna]], an alias of the famous [[archmage]] Iggwilv.<ref name="WBW-p19">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|19}}</ref> * Fablerise, the smaller domain of the archfey Yarnspinner, situated entirely within Prismeer.<ref name="DoD-p21" />

==Cosmology== In some versions of the [[Great Wheel cosmology]], the Domains of Dread were considered part of the [[Ethereal plane]],<ref name="RL-RT2e-p12" /> while other versions and the [[World Axis cosmology]] acknowledged them to be located in a remote, but easily accessible region of the Shadowfell.<ref name="DMG5e-p51" /><ref name="MotP4e-p50-51" /><ref name="CoS5e-p5,9">{{Cite book/Curse of Strahd|5,9}}</ref>
The mists that surrounded the domains prevented anyone caught inside from leaving through conventional means. In particular, many of the individual domains that made up the demiplanes had originally been locations in worlds of the [[Prime Material plane]], dragged and bound to the Shadowfell by the mists over a period of several centuries. Other locations, on the other hand, routinely collapsed or disappeared entirely. For that reason, it was impossible to determine the exact size of the domain.<ref name="CoS5e-p5,9" /><ref name="RL-RT2e-p13-15">{{Cite book/Ravenloft Campaign Setting/Realm of Terror|13-15}}</ref>
==Geography== The Demiplane of Dread was controlled by the almost completely unknown [[Dark Powers]] and sections of the demiplane were ruled over by dark lords.<ref name="DMG5e-p51" /> The ''Powers'' had no goals that anyone could confirm but seemed attracted to people and creatures that committed evil acts or suffered from some terrible loss. They regularly inflicted despair on the residents of the demiplane by simultaneously granting them boons and inflicting curses. Each curse was tailored to the individual and inflicted the greatest amount of emotional harm or distress upon them. This often spurred those individuals to commit greater acts of evil. It was apparent that the more heinous the deed, the greater the power and the worse the curse granted/inflicted upon the individual until a new land was generated on the demiplane and the individual was trapped forever within that land. These individuals became the Darklords, and they could never leave their domain. Others might be able to leave, but only if they had no great desire to, as the ''powers'' almost always intervened to dash the hopes of those trapped within their realm.{{Fact}}
==History== When [[Shar]] created the [[Shadowfell]], the Demiplane of Dread fragmented and each Darklord's realm settled into a spot somewhere within the newly created plane, possibly attracted by the plane's sinister nature. Within the Shadowfell, these realms became known as the '''Domains of Dread'''. Despite Shar's dominance of the Shadowfell, the Dark Powers still had control over each of these Domains.{{Fact}}
[[Castle Spulzeer]] in [[Tethyr]] was sucked into the demiplane by a magical gem set in the hilt of the dagger ''Aggarath''. [[Jander Sunstar]] suffered a similar fate after he swore revenge for his dead love,<ref name="VL-p36">{{Cite book/Villains' Lorebook|36}}</ref> and the Lost King of [[Cormyr]], [[Gondegal]], has gained a position of power as the leader of the Knight of the Shadows order, a secret society dedicated to the protection of the helpless and oppressed.<ref>{{Cite book/Champions of the Mists|47-49}}</ref>
Several residents of [[Faerûn]] have even risen to the level of Darklord: [[Harkon Lukas]], the [[cormyr]]ian [[wolfwere]];<ref name="RL-DD2e-p70-72">{{Cite book/Ravenloft Campaign Setting/Domains and Denizens|70-72}}</ref> [[Hazlik]], a [[red wizard]];<ref name="RL-DD2e-p66-67">{{Cite book/Ravenloft Campaign Setting/Domains and Denizens|66-67}}</ref> [[Urik von Kharkov]], an escaped magical experiment;<ref name="RL-DD2e-p94-97">{{Cite book/Ravenloft Campaign Setting/Domains and Denizens|94-97}}</ref> [[Draga Salt-Biter]], a [[Sword Coast]] pirate turned [[wereshark]];<ref name="IT2e-p38-50">{{Cite book/Islands of Terror|38-50}}</ref> and [[Tsien Chiang]], the renowned sorceress from [[Kara-Tur]].<ref name="IT2e-p32-37">{{Cite book/Islands of Terror|32-37}}</ref>
Over the centuries, the accounts of Torilians who entered the Domains of Dread and made it back were written down. Many of these [[book]]s found their way into [[Candlekeep]]. By the 15{{th}} century [[DR]], the Domains of Dread became rarely discussed by the sages of Candlekeep as the topic of the [[Spellplague]] and [[Second Sundering]] overtook them in prominence.<ref name="GG">{{Cite archive/Greenwood's Grotto/2023-02-25/Candlekeep's lore on other worlds}}</ref>
Sometime in the late 15th century DR, reports of [[werewolf]] attacks and [[Vistani]] sightings in [[Daggerford]] and surrounding areas indicated that a passage into one of the Domains of Dread might have been present somewhere in the [[Misty Forest]].<ref name="CoS-p19-22">{{Cite book/Curse of Strahd|19-22}}</ref>

{{Faction | faction = Doomguard | image1 = <gallery> FactionDoomguard5e.png|D&D 5e FactionDoomguard2e.png|AD&D 2e </gallery> | caption-image1 = | nickname = Sinkers | philosophy = Who Celebrate Destruction and Decay | founded = | factol = Factol [[Pentar]] | sigilhq = The [[Lady's Ward]]: The [[Armory]] | homefield = The negative quasiplanes ([[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Ash|Ash]], [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Dust|Dust]], [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Salt|Salt]], [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Vacuum|Vacuum]]) | allies = [[Bleak Cabal]], [[Heralds of Dust]] | enemies = [[Fraternity of Order]], [[Harmonium]] | predecessor = | successor = }}
The '''Doomguard''' are a [[faction]] who believe the multiverse is falling apart. It's ''supposed'' to fall apart. That's the natural order of things. That's entropy. Of course, a lot of deluded berks are trying to stop it, or at least slow it. The Doomguard want to stop them, and perhaps even ''hasten'' the course of entropy.
== History == * [[471 BFHR]]: The Doomguard start stockpiling weapons in the [[Armory]] to wage war in the streets of [[Sigil]].<ref name="fw33">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=33}}</ref> * [[21 BFHR]]: The Doomguard start stockpiling ''spheres of annihilation'' with the hopes to one day use them as tools of entropy.<ref name="fw58">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=58}}</ref> * [[122 YFHR]]: [[Pentar]] becomes [[factol]] of the Doomguard around this time.<ref name="fm41">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=41}}</ref>
Previous factols * Unnamed factol (immediately previous to Pentar, died in a slave uprising he sparked)<ref name="fm41">{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=41}}</ref>
== Philosophy == Entropy is ecstasy; decay is divine. The multiverse is ''supposed'' to fall apart. We're just here to keep leatherheads from interfering.
== Role ==
As they want to encourage the eventual destruction of the multiverse, the Doomguard are in charge of Sigil's [[Armory]], a building full of weapons with which to hasten the end.
== Membership ==
: ''See also:'' [[List of Doomguard members]]
The Sinkers don't really recognize much of a hierarchy (at least at lower levels) other than one's dedication to entropy: those who push hard for it, those who want to let the multiverse take its course, and those who want to slow down any progression. The first group are the most powerful force within the faction.
; '''[[Factor]]s'''
The most powerful and ruthless Sinkers are its factors, called ''Doomlords''. Doomlords are subjected to an unspeakable transformation in the [[Negative Energy plane]], and return wearing black-and-red masks. Doomlords sometimes create "champions of entropy", who are often given ''[[entropy blade]]s'', weapons forged to act against a specific threat to entropy. Once that threat has been defeated, the blade crumbles to dust.
There are many lesser Doomlords, but only four greater Doomlords, each of which is tied to a negative quasi-elemental plane, and largely oversees one of the faction's four Citadels.

==Synopsis== There are four 'blink portals' that appear in [[Sigil]] every 500 years and which last for two months. After this the portals disappear for another half-millennium. The overall aim is for the party to probe these portals and find out the secrets behind them. Rumors indicate that these doors lead to restricted planes, of hyper-real super-monsters, and that they were created by the god Aoskar when the [[Lady of Pain]] killed him.

=== Background Information === * While [[Dragon]] Magazine's "TSR Previews" section was generally very good at providing an up-to-date look at releases in the coming months, ''Doors to the Unknown'' apparently slipped under their radar entirely, and never showed up on their lists. Given that it released in 1996 after November's {{b|Planescape|A Guide to the Astral Plane|pdf=17287}}, we can reasonably guess that it released in December 1996. * TSR was deep in debt and sold themselves to Wizards of the Coast, meaning that this would be the final Planescape release before a seven-month production gap, resuming in July 1997 with the final part of the Blood Wars fiction trilogy, {{b|Planescape|The Blood Wars 3: Planar Powers}}. {{Plane | image = | caption = | name = Dragon Eyrie | othernames = | natives = [[Celestial creature|Celestial]] [[dragon]]s, [[Fiendish creature|fiendish]] dragons, [[planar dragon]]s, [[abishai]], [[khaasta]] | languages = | basicrefs = <ref name="PGtF-p150">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|150}}</ref> | type-GW = | shape-size-GW = | gravity-GW = | time-GW = | morphic-GW = | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = | magical-GW = | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = | refs-GW = | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = [[Neutral Plane]] | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = Alterable (each realm was divinely morphic) | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = Mildly good-aligned | magical-WT = | faith-WT = Mild | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = <ref name="PGtF-p140">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|140}}</ref><ref name="PGtF-p150" /> | inhabitants = yes | deities = yes | locations = yes | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = yes | useon = }} The '''Dragon Eyrie''' was the home of the [[Draconic pantheon]],<ref name="FRCS3e">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|258}}</ref> manifesting as a vast mountain with its peak eternally covered in frost and surrounded by wispy clouds.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
While the Dragon Eyrie was the home of all draconic deities, only [[Hlal]], [[Null]], [[Task]], and [[Tiamat]] had [[divine realm|permanent lairs]] on the plane.<ref name="PGtF-p150" /><ref group="note">When they were first introduced in the 2{{nd}} edition [[Draconomicon (1990)|''Draconomicon'']], the [[divine realm]]s of the various draconic deities were scattered throughout the planes: [[Asgorath]] on an unknown plane, [[Astilabor]] and [[Kereska]] in [[Limbo]], [[Garyx]] in the [[Abyss]], [[Hlal]] in [[Olympus]], [[Lendys]] in [[Nirvana]], [[Null]] in [[Gehenna]], [[Tamara]] on [[Elysium]], [[Task]] in [[Pandemonium]], [[Bahamut|Xymor]] in the [[Seven Heavens]], [[Zorquan]] on the [[Prime Material Plane]], and [[Tiamat]] in the [[Nine Hells]]. </ref>
==Dragon Eyrie Links== There were several "soft borders" connecting [[Tiamat]]'s realm in the Dragon Eyrie with [[Avernus]] on the plane of the [[Nine Hells]].<ref name="FRCS3e"/><ref name="FCII">{{Cite book/Fiendish Codex II: Tyrants of the Nine Hells|41}}</ref> Dragon Eyrie also contained links to [[Arvandor]].<ref name="FRCS3e"/><ref name="PGtF-p150" />
==Inhabitants== Around the mountain flew the spirits of departed dragons. Other departed souls whose destination was the Dragon's Eyrie included [[half-dragon]]s, [[dragonkin]], and other forms of [[dragonkind]]. [[Khaasta]] and [[abishai]] also dwelled on this plane, and living [[planar dragon]]s of all kinds visited the Eyrie from time to time. A few hermit non-dragons also inhabited the plane, although dragons only tolerated them grudgingly.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
==Divine Realms== The mountain was divided into four major regions: the dark roots, the lower reaches, the middle crags, and the peak. With the exception of the peak—which was entirely Null's divine realm—the divine realms were small regions and didn't occupy the whole of any given region. Most of the mountain was open territory without claim from any deity, where the petitioners of the plane sought solitude.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
===Hlal's Realm=== Hlal, trickster god and messenger deity, lived in the lower reaches with her [[brass dragon]] and [[copper dragon]] petitioners. The spirits of [[red dragon]]s, [[blue dragon]]s, and [[black dragon]]s lived in various portions of the lower reaches as well.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
===Null's Realm=== Null, god of death, ruled the entirety of the mountain's peak, along with [[white dragon]] and [[silver dragon]] petitioners attracted to the cold air and permanent snow cover.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
===Task's Realm=== Task, god of greed, lived in the middle reaches in a volcanic region known as the Furnace. The spirits of red, gold, and bronze dragons lived here as well, attracted by the heat and lava.<ref name="PGtF-p150" />
===Tiamat's Realm=== Tiamat's realm, originally the realm of a god known as [[Azharul]],<ref name="QfEG.2015-p7">{{Cite web/Candlekeep forum| title = Questions for Ed Greenwood (2015)| author = [[Ed Greenwood]]| topicid = 19841| postid = 464818| whichpage = 7| date = 2015-02-12| accessdate = 2015-02-16}}</ref> also called the ''Dragonspawn Pits of Azharul''<ref name="FCII"/> but renamed by Tiamat into the ''[[Cave of Greed]]'' after she killed the god,<ref name="QfEG.2015-p7"/><ref name="PGtF-p150" /> was the home of the spirits of [[chromatic dragon]]s who revered Tiamat above all others. Tiamat's realm existed in the depths of the plane, among the dark roots, where the spirits of [[shadow dragon]]s and [[deep dragon]]s also dwelt,<ref name="PGtF-p150" /> and was somehow connected to [[Tiamat's Lair|her lair]] in Avernus.<ref name="FRCS3e"/>
==History== The Dragon Eyrie was one of the planes destroyed by the [[Spellplague]].<ref name="QfEG.2015-p7"/>

== The Plane Truth, Part One: Codifying Sigil == : ''By [[David Cook|David "Zeb" Cook]], artwork by [[Dana Knutson]] and [[Tony DiTerlizzi]].'' '''p. 28-31'''
The article is presented as the unpublished journals of [[Ambran]] the Seeker, half-elven paladin of Oghma's temple at the court of [[Azoun IV]], King of Cormyr. Ambran refers often to the maps of the "Sage [[Trandleer]]," which seem to reflect 1st edition planar maps, e.g. from the {{b|D&D|Manual of the Planes}}. He notes the map's lack of locations like Sigil and the Palace of Judgment, and its incorrect names, such as the Concordant Opposition or the Nine Hells.
Volume 7 opens with Ambran, charged with exploring the planes, having spent ten days in [[Sigil]], and is now hiring a [[bariaur]] named [[Glin]] as a guide. Glin finds a portal from the [[Great Bazaar]] to the [[Palace of Judgment]].
After spending several days waiting in line only to be rebuffed at the entrance, Glin offers to take Ambran to [[Ribcage]].
: ''Volume 8 is lost, presumably in the flight from Ribcage, or the fight that followed.''
After escaping from Ribcage, the two pass through the [[Vale of the Spine]], past [[Rigus]], and to a field overlooking [[Automata]], just in time to witness the [[Great Modron March]]. There they meet up with a member of the [[Doomguard]], [[Rialiva]], who Ambran invites to join them on their way to the [[River Ma'at]].

== The Plane Truth, Part Three: The Transformation == : ''By [[David Cook|David "Zeb" Cook]], artwork by [[Dana Knutson]] and [[Tony DiTerlizzi]].'' '''p. 50-53'''
The article is presented as the final journal of [[Ambran]] the Seeker. Ambran has forsaken his god, name, and country to remain in the Outer Planes.
After spending several days at the [[Mausoleum of Chronepsis]], at [[Glin]]'s urging, Ambran opts to leave. As the approach and pass over [[Ilsensine]]'s [[Caverns of Thought]], Glin grows progressively more interested in Ambran's dreams. Ambran, perhaps overly-paranoid due to the persistent buzzing of Ilsensine's realm, lies. However, he does dream, of the [[Codex of Infinite Planes]]. In the dream, the book fills out with entries on locations, and Ambran is forced to go to those places. The book also builds an entry for a man named [[Fallendor]], and when the entry is complete, Fallendor will stand before him.
Ambran awakens to find the name "Fallendor" tattooed on his arm. Four days later, his arm is almost entirely covered. Two more days later, and they are visible around his neck. Glin seems afraid and no longer inquires about his dreams.
Ambran dreams more, apparently of Fallendor sending him the dreams, and gradually filling him up to be used as a host for the Codex. Ambran dismisses Glin from his service, with Glin apparently glad for it.
Ambran travels to [[Bedlam]], where he meets a [[shadowfiend]] named [[Hrava]], the leader of the [[Sarex]]. Hrava tells him that the Codex consumes someone via their dreams and makes them a slave -- and this slave is doing the same thing to Ambran, replacing him memory-by-memory, to escape the Codex.
Ambran continues from there to [[Pandemonium]].
Fallendor awakens in his new body, but with all his memories inscribed on his body, including his betrayal of Ambran, he remains shunned by everyone he encounters.
